lines.text: אבד 4 אבו
אֲבַד Chald. fut. יֵאבַד, to perish, Jer.
Aph. הוֹבַד, fut. יְהוֹבֵד, inf. הוֹבָדָה, to
destroy, to cut off, Dan. 2, 12. 18, 24.—
Hoph. הוּבַד, after the Heb. manner,
אֹבֵד m. 1. one wretched, unfortu-
nate; see r. אָבַד no. 3.
2. Participial noun, destruction, Num.
אֲבֵדָה f. (Tseri impure) 1. a thing
lost, something missing, Ex. 22, 8. Lev.
2. i. q. אֲבַדּוֹן place of destruction,
abyss, i. e. Sheol, Hades, Prov. 27, 20
Chethibh.
אֲבַדּוֹן m. 1. destruction, Job 31, 12.
2. place of destruction, abyss, nearly
synon. with שְׁאוֹל, Job 26, 6. 28, 22. Prov.
אַבְדָן m. verbal of Piel for אַבְּדָן, hence
without Dag. lene in ד, destruction,
slaughter, Esth. 9, 5.
אָבְדָן constr. אָבְדַן id. destruction
death, Esth. 8, 6.
* אָבָה fut. יֹאבֶה, pr. to breathe after,
to desire; comp. the kindred roots אָוָה,
יָאַב, תָּאַב, also אָהַב, חָבַב, Lat. aveo.—
Hence
1. to be willing, inclined, disposed; to
will, always with a negative partic. ex-
cept Is. 1, 19. Job 39, 9. Constr. c. infin.
either simpl. Deut. 2, 30. 10, 10. 25, 7. Is.
30, 9; or with לְ, which however be-
longs rather to prose, Lev. 26, 21. 2 Sam.
he would not let them go. Job 39, 9
הֲיֹאבֶה רֵּים עָבְדֶךָ will the buffalo be will-
ing to serve thee? Also c. acc. Prov. 1,
25; absol. Is. 1, 19 אִם תֹּאבוּ וּשְׁמַעְתֶּם if
ye be willing and obedient, lit. if ye con-
sent and obey; see in יָאַל Hiph. no. 2.
Prov. 1, 10. With dat. of pers. to be
willing towards any one, willing-mind-
ed, to obey (often with synon. שָׁמַע לְ),
2. to desire, i. e. to want, to need, a
signif. found in the derivatives אֲבוֹי,
אֶבְיוֹן, אֲבִיּוֹנָה.
Note. In Arabic this verb has the
sense to be unwilling, to refuse, to loathe,
corresponding to Heb. לֹא אָבָה. But this
must not be regarded as a contrary sig-
nification; since the idea of inclining,
which in Heb. implies towards any one,
expressing good will, Germ. Zuneigung,
is in Arabic merely referred to the oppo-
site direction, i. e. from or against any
one, expressing ill will, Germ. Abneigung,
i. e. aversion, loathing; whence مَأبِي
stinking swamp-water, pr. loathsome,
أَبَاءَةٌ a reed growing in marshes, bul-
rush; comp. אֲגַם, אַגְמוֹן.
Deriv. אֵבֶה, and those under no. 2.
אֵבֶה m. reed, bulrush, papyrus, i. q.
Arab. أَبَاءَةٌ, collect. أَبَاءٌ, see r. אָבָה
note; although the Heb. word might
come from the notion of a reed with its
top inclined, bowed down, comp. Is.
58, 5.—Once Job 9, 26 אֳנִיּוֹת אֵבֶה skiffs
of reed, i. e. boats or skiffs made of the
papyrus of the Nile, in common use
among the Egyptians and Ethiopians,
and famous for their lightness and swift-
ness; see Comment. on Is. 18, 2. Others
translate ships of desire, i. e. hasting
with eager desire to the haven, Symm.
ναυσὶ σπευδούσαις. The reading איבה,
which is exhibited in 44 Mss. is doubt-
less to be pronounced אֵיבָה, and to be
explained of hostile or robber-ships,
which likewise sail swiftly; this gives a
very good parallelism to the eagle in the
other hemistich pouncing upon his prey.
So the Syr. The same sense would also
be expressed by the common reading, if
for אֵבָה it were written אֶבָה.
אֲבוֹי m. (r. אָבָה no. 2) want, poverty,
wretchedness, once Prov. 23, 29; after the
form קָטוֹל, prob. for the sake of paro-
nomasia with the words אוֹי and הוֹי,
comp. Lehrg. p. 374 note r, and Is. 15,
4. 17, 1. 59, 13. So Abulwalid, whom
we do not hesitate to follow.—Kimchi,
who is followed by most interpreters,
makes it an exclamation of pain, O! wo!
like אוֹי and הוֹי. Comp. Gr. αἰβοῖ,
Arist. Pac. 1066.
אֵבוּס m. (r. אָבַס) by Syriasm for
אָבוּס, whence constr. אֵבוּס Is. 1, 3; plur.
אֲבוּסִים; a stall, stable, barn, where cat-
tle are fed Job 39, 9; and fodder stored
Prov. 14, 4. The signif. stall is also ap-
propriate in Is. 1, 3; where however Sept.

line_status.note: The last letter of the left-hand catchword has a flat top bar protruding right of the vertical stroke and no ascender above the line — a dalet (אבד), not a lamed; this also fits page 4 running from אבד to אבו.

The decisive difference is the vowel under the bet of the future form: the print shows two horizontal dots (tsere, יְהוֹבֵד), not a single patach stroke as in Reading A. The perfect הוֹבַד does have patach, and the infinitive הוֹבָדָה and the rest of the line are identical in both readings and match the print.

Both alephs carry a patah (horizontal stroke) — the first word is not qamets (A) and the second is not hiriq (B); the dot near each aleph is the adjacent shewa under bet. Second word has dagesh in bet.

Third word is אָהַב with he: the middle letter has a clear gap at the upper left between roofbar and left leg, unlike the closed ḥeth of the following חָבַב. Reading A's אָחַב is wrong; all other characters agree in both readings.
The resh of רֵּים is printed with a dagesh (the rare dagesh in resh of Job 39:9, which Gesenius reproduces); Reading B omits it. All other points and the English match.
The printed word has only four letters א־ב־ו־י with ḥolem on the vav and no final nun: it is אֲבוֹי, not אֶבְיוֹן (which is a separate derivative on the following line).

Printed left-to-right in the English flow: אֶבְיוֹן (final nun at far left of the line), comma, then אֲבִיּוֹנָה followed by the full stop — so אֶבְיוֹן is the first item and אֲבִיּוֹנָה the second, as in Reading B; Reading A reverses them. Pointing in both words matches (segol/sheva/holam-vav; hataf-patah/hiriq/dagesh-yod/holam-vav/qamats).

The Arabic carries fatha on mim, a hamza on the alif, and kasra under ba, but no sukun, and no shadda or tanwin on the final ya (Reading A over-points; Reading B drops the hamza). No space before the semicolon.
Both Arabic words carry a printed tanwīn ḍamma (ٌ) on the final letter — visible as the raised squiggle above the tā' marbūṭa and above the final hamza; Reading B omits these case endings.
The Hebrew איבה is printed unpointed — no tsere under the aleph and no qamets under the bet are visible; Reading B supplies vowels that are not on the page.

Both words carry qamets under the bet; the first word has tsere (two dots) under the aleph, the second has segol (three dots) under the aleph — neither hateph-pathach (A) nor qamets/segol as placed in B.

The point under the first aleph is a qamets (bar with stem), not hateph-pataḥ; consistent with the headword אֵבוּס being 'by Syriasm for אָבוּס'. A also preserves the printed space before the semicolon in '3 ;'. (Print also has a small gap before the comma after אָבוּס — spacing only.)
The aleph carries a ḥaṭef pataḥ (shva + short horizontal stroke), not a tsere (two horizontal dots), so Reading B is correct; no space is printed before the semicolon.
